{{Use dmy dates|date=December 2024}}
In [[stochastic calculus]], the '''Ogawa integral''', also called the '''non-causal stochastic integral''', is a [[stochastic integral]] for [[Adapted process|non-adapted processes]] as [[integrand]]s. The corresponding calculus is called '''non-causal calculus''' which distinguishes it from the anticipating calculus of the [[Skorokhod integral]]. The term causality refers to the adaptation to the [[natural filtration]] of the integrator.

The integral was introduced by the Japanese mathematician [[Shigeyoshi Ogawa]] in 1979.<ref>{{cite journal |first=Shigeyoshi |last=Ogawa |title=Sur le produit direct du bruit blanc par lui-même |journal=C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris Sér. A |publisher=Gauthier-Villars |volume=288 |pages=359–362 |date=1979}}</ref>

== Ogawa integral ==
Let
* <math>(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)</math> be a [[probability space]],
* <math>W=(W_t)_{t\in[0,T]}</math> be a one-dimensional standard [[Wiener process]] with <math>T\in\mathbb{R}_+</math>,
* <math>\mathcal{F}_t^W=\sigma(W_s;0\leq s \leq t)\subset \mathcal{F}</math> and <math>\mathbf{F}^W=\{\mathcal{F}_t^W, t\geq 0\}</math> be the natural filtration of the Wiener process,
* <math>\mathcal{B}([0,T])</math> the [[Borel σ-algebra]],
* <math>\int f\; dW_t</math> be the Wiener integral,
* <math>dt</math> be the [[Lebesgue measure]].

Further let <math>\mathbf{H}</math> be the set of real-valued processes <math>X\colon [0,T]\times \Omega \to\mathbb{R}</math> that are  <math>\mathcal{B}([0,T])\times \mathcal{F}</math>-measurable and [[almost surely]] in <math>L^2([0,T],dt)</math>, i.e.
:<math>P\left(\int_0^T |X(t,\omega)|^2 \, dt< \infty\right)=1.</math>

=== Ogawa integral ===
Let <math>\{\varphi_n\}_{n\in \mathbb{N}}</math> be a [[Orthonormal basis#Incomplete orthogonal sets|complete]] [[orthonormal basis]] of the [[Hilbert space]] <math>L^2([0,T],dt)</math>.

A process <math>X\in\mathbf{H}</math> is called <math>\varphi</math>-integrable if the random series
:<math>\int_0^T X_t \, d_\varphi W_t:=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(\int_0^T X_t \varphi_n(t) \, dt\right) \int_0^T\varphi_n(t) \, dW_t</math>
[[Convergence of random variables#Convergence in probability|converges in probability]] and the corresponding sum is called the '''Ogawa integral''' with respect to the basis <math>\{\varphi_n\}</math>.

If <math>X</math> is <math>\varphi</math>-integrable for any complete orthonormal basis of <math>L^2([0,T],dt)</math> and the corresponding integrals share the same value then <math>X</math> is called '''universal Ogawa integrable''' (or '''u-integrable''').<ref name="Ogawa2007">{{cite journal |first=Shigeyoshi |last=Ogawa |date=2007 |title=Noncausal stochastic calculus revisited – around the so-called Ogawa integral |journal=Advances in Deterministic and Stochastic Analysis |isbn=978-981-270-550-1 |doi=10.1142/9789812770493_0016 |page=238}}</ref>

More generally, the Ogawa integral can be defined for any <math>L^2(\Omega,P)</math>-process <math>Z_t</math> (such as the [[fractional Brownian motion]]) as integrators
:<math>\int_0^T X_t \, d_\varphi Z_t:=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(\int_0^T X_t \varphi_n(t) \, dt\right) \int_0^T\varphi_n(t) \, dZ_t</math>
as long as the integrals
:<math>\int_0^T\varphi_n(t) \, dZ_t</math>
are well-defined.<ref name="Ogawa2007" />

==== Remarks ====
* The convergence of the series depends not only on the orthonormal basis but also on the ordering of that basis.
* There exist various equivalent definitions for the Ogawa integral which can be found in (<ref name="Ogawa2007" />{{rp|239–241}}). One way makes use of the [[Itô–Nisio theorem]].

==== Regularity of the orthonormal basis ====
An important concept for the Ogawa integral is the ''regularity'' of an orthonormal basis. An orthonormal basis <math>\{\varphi_n\}_{n\in \mathbb{N}}</math> is called ''regular'' if
:<math>\sup_n \int_0^T \left( \sum_{i=1}^n \varphi_i(t)\int_0^t \varphi_i(s) \, ds\right)^2 \, dt<\infty</math>
holds.

The following results on regularity are known:
* Every [[semimartingale]] (causal or not) is <math>\varphi</math>-integrable if and only if <math>\{\varphi_n\}</math> is regular.<ref name="Ogawa2007" />{{rp|242–243}}
* It was proven that there exist a non-regular basis for <math>L^2([0,1], dt)</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Pietro |last1=Majer |first2=Maria Elvira |last2=Mancino |title=A counter-example concerning a condition of Ogawa integrability|journal=Séminaire de probabilités de Strasbourg |volume=31 |date=1997 |pages=198–206 |url=http://www.numdam.org/item/SPS_1997__31__198_0/ |access-date=26 June 2023}}</ref>

== Further topics ==
* There exist a non-causal [[Itô formula]],<ref name="Ogawa2007" />{{rp|250}} a non-causal integration by parts formula and a non-causal [[Girsanov theorem]].<ref>{{cite journal |first=Shigeyoshi |last=Ogawa |title=BPE and a Noncausal Girsanov's Theorem |journal=Sankhya A |volume=78 |pages=304–323 |date=2016 |issue=2 |doi=10.1007/s13171-016-0087-x|s2cid=258705123 }}</ref>

=== Relationship to other integrals ===
* [[Stratonovich integral]]: let <math>X</math> be a continuous <math>\mathbf{F}^W</math>-adapted semimartingale that is universal Ogawa integrable with respect to the Wiener process, then the Stratonovich integral exist and coincides with the Ogawa integral.<ref>{{cite journal|first1=David|last1=Nualart|first2=Moshe|last2=Zakai|title=On the Relation Between the Stratonovich and Ogawa Integrals|journal=The Annals of Probability|volume=17|number=4|pages=1536–1540|date=1989|doi=10.1214/aop/1176991172|url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/annals-of-probability/volume-17/issue-4/On-the-Relation-Between-the-Stratonovich-and-Ogawa-Integrals/10.1214/aop/1176991172.full|hdl=1808/17063|hdl-access=free}}</ref>
* [[Skorokhod integral]]: the relationship between the Ogawa integral and the Skorokhod integral was studied in (<ref>{{cite journal |first1=David |last1=Nualart |first2=Moshe |last2=Zakai |title=Generalized stochastic integrals and the Malliavin calculus |journal=Probability Theory and Related Fields |volume=73 |number=2 |pages=255–280 |date=1986| doi=10.1007/BF00339940|s2cid=120687698 |doi-access=free }}</ref>).
